questionStem: A 68-year-o ld man comes to the physician because of a 1-month history of increasingly severe pain in his legs. He describes the pain as an ache that radiates to both calves. The pain becomes increasingly severe when he walks more than three blocks and resolves with rest. He has an 8-year history of low back pain after a fall from a ladder. His only medication is ibuprofen. He has smoked one-half pack of cigarettes daily for 45 years. He drinks two 12-oz beers daily. His temperatu re is 37°C (98.6 °F), pulse is 86/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 138/92 mm Hg. Examination shows mild edema of the lower extremities. There is a small effusion over both knees but no erythema or tenderness to palpation. The shins are cool to the touch. Crossed straight-leg raising test is negative, and deep tendon reflexes are 2+ bilaterally. Pedal pulses are 1 + and equal bilaterally. Capillary refill time is 3 seconds in both feet. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Determination of ankle brachia! indices (ABI) is the next most appropriate step in diagnosis for this patient with exertional leg pain that improves with rest. His symptoms are most consistent with claudication from peripheral vascular disease (PVD). The ABI is a noninvasive means of assessing for PVD and can be performed in the clinic. It is commonly calculated by dividing the systolic blood pressure in the lower extremity at the ankle by the systolic blood pressure in the arm at the level of the brachia! artery. A ratio of less than 0.9 indicates the presence of occlusive arterial vascular disease while a ratio between 0.9 and 1.3 is suggestive of normal arteries. An ABI above 1.3 likely indicates the presence of calcified vesse ls and also necessitates further evaluation for vascular disease. Further evaluation may include the use of duplex ultrasonography or CT angiography. All patients with claudication and confirmed PVD should be started on a statin and antiplatelet agent. Exercise programs are often effective in improving exercise tolerance, increasing neovascularization and collateral flow, and diminishing symptoms.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Arthrocentesis of both knees (Choice A) is not indicated. This patient's calf pain that worsens with exercise and improves with rest is suggestive of PVD. MRI of the lumbar spine (Choice C) would be appropriate for patients suspected of having neurogenic claudication. Symptoms of neurogenic claudication can mimic those of PVD, but patients often experience relief of pain with leaning forward and worsening of the pain with lying supine or standing. Additionally, this patient has no lower extremity neurologic deficits. - - - - . - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - .

questionStem: A 35-year-o ld woman who has been a patient for several years comes to the office because a pregnancy test done at home was positive. The pregnancy is confirmed by physical examination. During the past 5 months, she had two visits to the emergency department for traumatic injuries, each of which she attributed to her own clumsiness. She is married and has four children. Reluctantly, she reports concern about her personal safety and, with great embarrassment, confesses that the emergency department visits were precipitated by her husband hitting and pushing her. She says that she is afraid he will hurt her if she leaves him or if he finds out she is pregnant again. He lost his job nearly 1 year ago. She says that he is abusive only when he has been drinking. She tearfully asks to be referred to someone who can terminate her pregnancy. Which of the following is the most accurate statement concerning the patient's situation?

choices.A: Her husband's behavior is a logical consequence of his job loss
choices.B: Her pregnancy increases her risk for abuse
choices.C: Hiding all liquor in the house will reduce her risk for abuse
choices.D: Marital therapy is usually helpful in reducing the risk for violence
choices.E: Termination of the pregnancy will increase her risk for abuse

correctExplanation: Domestic abuse or intimate partner violence (IPV) may involve episodes of verbal, sexual, financia l, emotional, and/or physica l abuse. Risk factors for IPV are a combination of intersect ing individual, relationship, community, and societal factors. Examples of risk factors for victims include female sex, alcohol use or drug use, unemployment, poverty, history of depression or mental illness, and relationships characterized by dominance and control or excessive jealousy. Risk factors for perpetrators incl ude exposure to childhood violence, recent job loss or instability, and substance use. It has been shown that IPV often increases or begins during pregnancy, especially unintended pregnancies. IPV is often difficult to diagnose as a result of patients often concealing abusive relationships; signs may be subtle or absent. Inconsisten t explanation of injuries, delay in seeking treatmen t, and frequent emergency department visits increase suspicion for IPV.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. IPV and physical abuse are never acceptable and would not be a logical consequence of his job loss (Choice A), though job loss as a stressor may precipitate episodes. Hiding all liquor in the house will reduce her risk for abuse (Choice C) is incorrect. While substance use increases the risk for IPV occurrence, it is not a direct cause of IPV, and hiding all liquor in the house would not necessarily reduce her risk for abuse. Marital therapy is usually helpful in reducing the risk for violence (Choice D) is incorrect. Marital therapy is unlikely to reduce the risk for violence. Interventions for perpetrators are often minimal ly successful, and therapy has not been conclusively shown to reduce the risk

questionStem: An 18-month-old girl is brought to the phys ician by her mother for a routine examination. She was born at 32 weeks ' gestation by cesarean delivery because of maternal preeclamps ia. Apgar scores were 5 and 6 at 1 and 5 minutes, respec tively. She was in the neona tal intensive care unit for 2 days because of fetal lung immaturity; she progressed well and was discharged at 1 week of age. She was exclusively breast-fed until the age of 6 months, when pureed foods were added to her diet. She was weaned off breast milk at the age of 14 months; at that time, soft foods and whole milk, which she tolerates well, were added to her diet. She receives no medicat ions. Results of a complete blood count and measurement of blood lead concentrat ion at the age of 1 year were within the reference ranges . She appears healthy. She is at the 25th percenti le for length, 5th percentile for weight, and 25th percentile for head circumference . Vital signs are within normal limits. Exam ination shows no abnorma lities. Screening for which of the following deficie ncies is most appropriate at this time?
correctExplanation: Iron is potentially deficient in this patient. Prematu re infants are at an increased risk for iron deficiency than infants born at term . In utero, fetuses begin to develop iron stores in the last trimester of gestation, so premature birth reduces the time available for children to develop iron stores. Additionally, preterm infants who have spent time in the neonatal intensive care unit are at a greater risk for iron depletion from frequent blood draws, which reduce their already insufficient iron stores. In these patients, iron stores usually become insufficien t within about 4 months without proper supplementation, so all patients should be screened for iron deficiency. Furthe rmore, breast milk contains little iron, so premature infants who are exclusive ly breast- fed are at even higher risk. Supplementation for children who are deficient is with oral iron.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Calcium (Choice A) deficiency in otherwise healthy infants is rare. Hypocalcemia can be seen in cases of DiGeorge syndrome. Folic acid (Choice B) deficiency is rare as folate is present in breast milk. Most mothers who take folate supplements in the form of prenatal vitamins throughout their pregnancy usually have adequate stores for breast-feeding infants. Vitamin B 12 (cobalamin) (Choice D) stores in an infant are dependent upon sufficient stores in the breast-feeding mother. Most women who receive prenatal care and take a prenatal vitamin are replete in vitamin B 12. - -- - . - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -- -- - - - - -- - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -- - .

questionStem: A 17-year-old boy is brought to the physician shortly after injuring his right ankle during a high school football game. He says that his ankle "turned in" while he was trying to make a tackle. He was able to limp off the field and can bear weight on the ankle. Examination of the right ankle shows moderate swelling over the area distal to the lateral malleolus. The area is tender to palpation. There is no bony point tenderness. Joint testing shows no instability. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in manageme nt?

choices.A: Apply ice and advise periodic leg elevation
choices.B: Apply topical capsaicin cream to the tender area
choices.C: Immobilize the ankle in a short-leg walking cast
choices.D: Inject a cortisone and lidocaine mixture into the tender area
choices.E: Order x-rays of the ankle and foot

correctExplanation: Ankle sprain is a common sports injury in which a ligament is stretched or torn. Ankle sprains are particular ly common among young athletes and are frequently sustained while twisting a planted foot or landing a jump. Lateral ankle sprains of the anterior talofibular ligament are the most common and are encountered when a plantar-flexed foot is inverted. Mild or moderate sprains involve stretching or mild tearing of a ligament, and are accompanied by pain, swel ling, and tenderness over the affected ligament. Severe sprains involve a complete tear and are accompanied by mechanical instability and loss of weight-bearing ability and motion of the affected joint. The Ottawa Ankle Rules can be used to assess the likelihood of accompanying fractures and the need for plain x-rays. They include focal tenderness at particular locations (the posterior edge of the lateral malleolus or medial malleolus, the navicular bone, and the base of the fifth metatarsa l) and the patient's ability to bear weight. Most patients with ankle sprains do not benefit from x-ray imaging. Ultrasonography may be useful for assessing the integrity of a ligament. Most patients with ankle sprains improve with conservative management, including rest, application of ice, compression, and elevation of the affected joint.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Application of topical capsaicin cream (Choice B) is useful for neuropathic pain in the setting of diabetic polyneuropathy or post-herpetic neuralgia. It is not typical ly useful for the treatment of acute pain associated with sprains. Immobilization of the ankle in a short-leg walking cast (Choice C) may occasionally be used in patients with severe ankle sprains. Patients with mild or moderate sprains may benefit from an elastic wrap or stirrup but do not require casting. Injection of a cortisone and lidocaine mixture into the tender area (Choice D) is not necessary for most patients with mild ankle sprains. Additiona lly, steroids can impair healing of tendons and ligaments.

questionStem: A 61-yea r-old woman comes to the office in July for a routine exam inatio n. She has hypertensio n and major depressive disorder. Her medications are hydroch loroth iazide and citalopram. She does not smoke cigarettes. Her blood pressure is 122/78 mm Hg; other vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows no abnorma lities. Which of the follow ing is the most approp riate vacci ne at this time?
correctExplanation: Varicella zoster virus infection, also known as shingles or herpes zoster, commonly presents as a painful, unilateral, dermatomal erythematous patch with overlying clear to yellow, grouped vesicles. It is caused by varicella-zoster virus, also known as human herpesvirus-3, which is transmitted via respiratory secretions and direct contact with infected skin lesions. It can be associated with neuropathic pain which can both precede and outlast the rash, which is more common in elderly patients. The Center for Disease Control recommends a herpes zoster vaccine to prevent varicella zoster virus infection for people 60 years of age or older. It is a live virus vaccine and is indicated in this patient who is 61 years old. It may be given regardless of history of varicella zoster virus infection, as infection can recur.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Human papillomavirus (HPV) (Choice B) is sexually transmitted and is associated with genital warts along with premalignant and malignant lesions of the cervical, anogenital, and oropharyngeal regions. HPV vaccines have significantly decreased the incidence and prevalence of HPV and protect against HPV-related malignancies such as cervical and anal squamous cell carcinoma. The vaccine should be administered ideally before the teenage years, as the immune response is most robust before the teenage years and the onset of sexual activity may occur during the teenage years. Influenza (Choice C) is a respiratory viral illness that can be comp licated by lower respiratory tract infection and bacterial superinfection, especially in elderly patients. Influenza is a seasonal illness, affecting patients typically in winter and early spring months. It would not be appropriate to give an influenza vaccine in July. Meningococcal (Choice D) vaccine is indicated for all children, with an additional serogroup B vaccine indicated for all patients over 10 years old at increased risk for meningococcal disease (eg, dormitory, military living).

questionStem: A previous ly healthy 42-yea r-old man comes to the physician because of right low back pain that began 2 days ago after he cleaned his garage. The pain radiates to the right buttock and posterior aspect of the right lower extremity to below the knee. He rates the pain as an 8 on a 10-point scale. It is worse when he is sitting. He has not had any other neurologic symptoms. He is visibly in pain as he tries to climb onto the examination table. His temperatu re is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 92/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 142/88 mm Hg. There is straightening of the lumbar lordosis and tenderness to percussion over L4-5. Muscle strength is 5/5, and deep tendon reflexes and sensation are intact and symmetric. Straight-leg raise testing is positive on the right at 40 degrees with pain radiating down the right leg. Straight-leg raise testing is positive on the left at 45 degrees with pain radiating down the right leg. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.F: Use of a lumbar support brace

correctExplanation: Lumbar disc herniation occurs most often following chronic disc degeneration combined with a minor traumat ic event such as bending and lifting a heavy object causing an acute increase in the intradiscal pressure. Disc herniation typically presents as acute back pain along with symptoms of lumbosacral radiculopathy, including acute extremity pain or weakness in a dermatomal and myotomal distribution with respect to the impinged spinal nerve. The diagnosis of lumbar disc herniation is clinical and can be made through a combination of history and various examination maneuvers, including the straight leg raise test (in which flexion of the hip while the leg is held in extension at the knee reproduces pain in the lower back that generally shoots down the leg). Lumbar imaging with MRI or CT scan is useful for patients with severe motor or sensory dysfunction but is not required for most patients with mild or moderate symptoms without an objective neurologic deficit and in whom there is no concern for spinal cord impingement. Patients with evidence of myotomal muscular weakness may benefit from nerve conduction studies or electromyography. Lumbosacral radiculopathy secondary to lumbar disc herniation is typically a self-limited process, with most patients demonstrating spontaneous improvement with conservative management, including analgesia, physical therapy, and normal activity as tolerated. Prolonged bed rest is not necessary for most patients and may worsen pain and prolong recovery.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Bed rest for 3 days (Choice A) may worsen pain and prolong recovery. Most patients are able to immediately resume normal activity as tolerated with symptomatic control.

questionStem: A large, multisite family medicine practice is planning a point-of-care ultrasonography screening program for abdomina l aortic aneurysms in men age 65 to 75 years with a history of smoking. A pilot study of 100 patients in the practice group found point-of-care ultrasonography had the following results: Sensitivity 90% Specificity 90% Positive predictive value 36 Negative predictive value 99 Positive likelihood ratio 9.00 Negative likelihood ratio 0.11 The practice's prevalence of abdominal aneurysm was estimated at 6% for this age group and gender. If the actual practice prevalence of aortic aneurysm is 5%, which of the following would decrease?
correctExplanation: If the practice prevalence of abdominal aortic aneurysm is only 5%, not the estimated 6%, then the positive predictive value of the point-of-care ultrasound will decrease. The pretest probability, or the baseline risk for having the condition of interest, in this case abdominal aortic aneurysm, is proportionate to the prevalence of disease in the population that will be tested. Pretest probability is important because it impacts the positive predictive value (PPV) and negative predictive value (NPV) of a test. PPV and NPV are statistical measures that define the proportion of positive test results that are true positives (positive tests in patients who have the condition) and true negatives (negative tests in patients without the condition). Both PPV and NPV vary with disease prevalence; PPV varies directly with prevalence whereas NPV varies inversely with prevalence. Therefore, the less prevalent a disease, the lower the PPV of a test used in that population and the higher the NPV of a test used in that population. In contrast, pretest probability does not impact the sensitivity or specificity of a test.
incorrectExplanation: nd F.

questionStem: A previous ly healthy 15-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of a 2-day history of runny nose and nonproductive cough and a 1-day history of irritation and tearing of both eyes. The patient's temperature is 36.7°C (98°F); other vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows a small amount of crusty discharge over the eyelids. The conjunct ivae are injected. There is no photophobia. Visual acuity is 20/20 bilatera lly. There is a small amount of clear nasal discharge. The lungs are clear to auscultation. Which of the following is the most appropr iate next step in management?
correctExplanation: Viral conjunctivitis presents with bilateral follicular conjunctivitis, tearing, blurry vision, and irritation. Symptoms typically begin in one eye prior to spreading to the contralateral eye. Patients may also note a coincident or recent upper respiratory tract infection and may have symptoms of fever, rhinorrhea, and preauricular or submandibular lymphadenopathy. Epidemic keratoconjunctivitis, a severe form of viral conjunctivitis, presents with photophobia, subepithelial corneal inflammatory infiltrates, and a profound conjunctivitis characterized by the presence of conjunctiva! pseudomembranes. Adenoviruses are the most commonly implicated in the pathogenesis of viral conjunctivitis, although most patients do not require conjunctiva! swabs for polymerase chain reaction test. The majority of patients improve with conservative symptomatic treatment only, including lubricating eye drops and cool compresses. Patients with epidemic keratoconjunctivitis benefit from treatment with topical steroids. Viral conjunctivitis is highly contagious, and patients should be counseled to stay home from work or school and to wash their hands frequently.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Culture of the ocular discharge (Choice A) is not typically required, as it will not impact management for most patients given that viral conjunctivitis is a self-limited condition. Culture of the ocular discharge may be helpful for patients with bacterial conjunctivitis. Oral doxycycline therapy (Choice B) is helpful for the treatment of conjunctivitis caused by Chlamydia trachomatis. Chlamydia! conjunctivitis may resemble viral conjunctivitis in the acute phase but typically presents a more chronic course. Topical acyclovir therapy (Choice D) may be used to treat herpetic viral conjunctivitis. Herpetic conjunctivitis is typically accompanied by vesicular skin lesions and corneal dendritic lesions.

questionStem: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the office by his parents because of a 2-day history of increasingly severe right lower abdomina l pain and nausea. He has not had fever, vomiting, or diarrhea. He receives no medications . He recently emigrated with his family from Libya to the USA. He appears to be in mild distress . His temperatu re is 37.2°C (99.0°F), pulse is 90/min and regular, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg. Abdominal examinat ion shows tenderness to palpation of the right lower quadrant with no rebound, guarding, or masses. The remainder of the exam ination shows no abnormalities. Laboratory studies are shown: Hemoglob in 8.2 g/dL (N=11.5-14.5) Mean corpuscu lar hemoglobin 20 pg/cell (N=25-31) Mean corpuscu lar volume 65 µm3 (N=76-90) Leukocyte count 8600/mm3 (with a normal differentia l) Urinalysis shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is most likely to confirm the underly ing diagnosis?

choices.E: Examination of the stool for ova and parasites

correctExplanation: A blood smear is most likely to confirm the underlying diagnosis of sickle cell disease (SCD). This patient has a microcytic anemia with lower quadrant abdominal pain, which is concerning for an acute pain crisis secondary to SCD. While other intra-abdominal pathology such as intussusception or appendicitis should be considered, the presence of sickle cells on the peripheral smear would strongly favor SCD as the cause of his pain. Additiona lly, the absence of fever or leukocytosis lowers the probability of an intra-abdomina l infection. Patients with sickle cell crisis may develop pain secondary to vase-occlusive events in nearly any part of the body, but acute abdomina l pain and dactylitis are particularly common in children. Treatment should focus on aggressive management of pain with the use of opiate and non-opiate medications and reversing any cause that may have triggered the pain crisis (eg, infection, acidosis, volume depletion). Patients with pain crises often respond to the administration of fluids as well as analgesics. Patients with frequent pain episodes should be considered for the use of hydroxyurea. Based on his age, this patient will also require evaluation for vaccination with consideration of splenic function and potentially prophylaxis against opportunistic infectious organisms.

questionStem: A 45-year-o ld man with hypertension and sleep apnea comes to the office for a follow-up visit 4 weeks after an evaluation for polydipsia and polyuria disclosed a nonfasting serum glucose concentration of 220 mg/dl, an LDL-choleste rol concentration of 200 mg/dl, and hemoglobin A 1c of 8.5%. His only medicat ion is lisinopril. The patient was advised to begin using a non-invasive positive pressure airway machine three months ago but does not use the machine nightly as recomme nded. During the initial evaluation, the patient was counseled on lifestyle modifications including weight loss, diet, and exercise. He has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for the past 30 years and works as a stockbroker. He is 178 cm (5 ft 10 in) tall and weighs 120 kg (265 lb); BMI is 38 kg/m2. His blood pressure is 150/92 mm Hg; the remainder of vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows no abnorma lities. In addition to initiating metformin therapy, which of the following is the most appropr iate recomme ndation for this patient?

choices.A: Adjustment of medication to achieve target blood pressure
choices.B: Adjustment of medication to achieve target hemoglobin A 1c
choices.C: Examination of the feet in the office every 3 to 4 months
choices.D: Ophtha lmologic exam ination every 3 years

correctExplanation: Adjustment of medication to achieve target blood pressure is the correct answer. This patient has type 2 diabetes mellitus and has been initiated on metformin therapy, which is first line therapy for patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus and normal kidney function. The goal blood pressure for patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus is less than 130/80 mm Hg as this is correlated with a reduction in cardiovascular morbidity and mortality, thus this patient's blood pressure reading of 150/92 mm Hg is above goal. He is already on lisinopril, which is an angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor (ACEi) and is an appropriate medication choice for patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension, especially those with any degree of proteinuria. The next step would be to increase this patient's lisinopril or add a second medication such as a calcium channel blocker or thiazide diuretic to achieve a blood pressure less than 130/80 mm Hg.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Adjustment of medication to achieve target hemoglobin A 1c (Choice B) would be premature as this patient was just diagnosed with diabetes mellitus 1 month ago. The A1c is an average of the blood glucose over 3 months and should be checked again in 2 months. Examination of the feet in the office every 3 to 4 months (Choice C) is incorrect. A dedicated foot examination with monofilament testing is indicated once yearly, although the patient's feet should be checked for onychomycosis or ulcers at every visit. Ophthalmologic examination every 3 years (Choice D) is incorrect. Patients with diabetes mellitus should have their eyes examined for evidence of retinopathy once yearly.

questionStem: A popular 17-year-o ld high school student witnessed an argume nt betwee n her present boyfrie nd and a previous boyfrie nd. She then ran away from home with her best friend and used excessive amou nts of alco hol for 3 days. Throug hout this period, she maintained her honors schoolwork and her after-school job. Which of the following is the most likely diag nosis?
correctExplanation: Adjustment disorder can present with symptoms of depression, anxiety or behaviora l changes after an identifiable psychosocial stressor such as divorce or illness, and typically lasts less than 6 months. It generally causes significantly impaired functioning in daily life. This patient is presenting with acute behavioral change after a recent stressor, but her behavior has not appeared to significantly impair her function, as she has maintained schoolwork and her after-school job. Treatment for adjustment disorder can involve cognitive behavioral therapy or selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors. Cognitive behaviora l therapy is a form of psychosocial therapy that focuses on challenging harmfu l though ts, beliefs, attitudes, and behaviors, and developing coping strategies.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Alcohol dependence (Choice B) is characterized by chronic alcohol intake characterized by increased tolerance and symptoms of withdrawa l with intake cessation. This patient's alcohol intake appears acute and related to a recent stressor. It would be unlikely for this patient to experience withdrawa l symptoms after intake is stopped. Conduct disorder (Choice C) refers to persistent emotional and behavioral problems such as purposeful aggression toward people and animals in children and adolescents. The behavioral problems can include lying and serious rule violations. This patient does not display aggression toward others and her behavior is acutely following a stressor, making adjustment disorder more likely. Panic disorder (Choice D) features panic attacks that occur unexpectedly and are associated with changes in behavior to avoid panic attack triggers. This patient is unlikely experiencing recurrent panic attacks consistent with panic disorder. Panic attacks feature acute fear or anxiety that peaks within minutes and is associated with additional physica l symptoms or associated menta l states including palpitations, shortness of breath, chest pain, dizziness, the sensation of choking, gastrointestinal distress, paresthesias, sweating, chills, trembling, derealization, the fear of dying, or the fear of losing control. - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - .

questionStem: A previous ly healthy 12-year-o ld boy is brought to the physician because of a 1-week history of sore throat and fatigue. His temperature is 38.1 °C (100.5°F); other vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows enlarged tonsils and pharyngea l erythema and exudates. The anterior cervical lymph nodes are tender to palpation. A complete blood count shows leukocytosis and atypical lymphocytes. A rapid streptococca l test is negative. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?

choices.D: Oral aspirin as needed for feve

correctExplanation: Infectious mononucleosis is a viral illness caused most often by infection with Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), which is transmitted through respiratory secretions and saliva, causing it to be commonly acquired by teenagers and young adults. It presents with fatigue, malaise, fever, chills, and sore throat. Physical examination may disclose hepatosplenomegaly, posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, or pharyngitis with erythema and exudates. Laboratory evaluation will demonstrate leukocytosis with atypical lymphocytes and, occasiona lly, increased transaminases. Diagnosis can be made with the Monospot test, which detects heterophi le antibodies through the agglutination of sheep or horse erythrocytes. Treatment is supportive and patients should be counseled to avoid any contact sports until the splenomegaly has resolved as a result of the risk for splenic rupture. If amoxici llin is administered for treatment of a misdiagnosed pharyngitis thought to be from S. pyogenes, patients may develop a characteristic, generalized maculopapular rash. Therefore, in this patient, viscous lidocaine gargle for throat pain is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Intramuscular ceftriaxone (Choice A) can be used to treat gonococcal pharyngitis, which presents with sore throat, erythema and exudates, and cervical lymphadenopathy. It is commonly acquired via receptive oral sex. Gonococcal pharyngitis does not cause an atypical lymphocytosis. Oral acyclovir (Choice B) can be used in the treatment or prevention of herpes simplex virus infections. Infectious mononucleosis is caused by EBV, which does not characteristica lly respond to treatment with acyclovir. Oral amoxicillin (Choice C) can be used to treat streptococca l pharyngitis. When given in infectious mononucleosis, it may cause a generalized maculopapu lar rash. This patient's rapid streptococcal test was negative, making infectious mononucleosis a more likely diagnosis.

questionStem: A 13-year-old girl is brought to the office by her mother for a routine well-child examinat ion. She began menstruating 1 year ago. She eats healthy food including vegetables. She plays tennis and soccer, sleeps well, and has a supportive network of friends. She is getting straight A's in school. The patient has a bright affect. Vital signs are within normal limits and physical examination shows no abnormal ities. The physician provides counseling about accident prevention, drugs, safe sex, and use of helmets when riding a bicycle or scooter. Counse ling about which of the following additional topics should be provided at this visit?

choices.D: Vitamin D and folic acid supplementation
choices.E: No additiona l counseling is necessary

correctExplanation: All well-child examinations of adolescents should include screening for depression and discussion of suicide prevention. Suicide is becoming more preva lent in adolescents and is the third leading cause of death in this age group. Risk factors associated with suicide include increased rates of substance use, major depressive disorder, access to firearms, and social and family challenges. There are various screening tools which identify patients at risk for major depressive disorder. A diagnosis of major depressive disorder is made when a patient experiences five or more of the following symptoms over a 2-week period or greater: depressed mood, anhedonia, change in appetite or weight, insomnia or hypersomnia, psychomotor agitation or retardation, fatigue, feelings of worth lessness, diminished ability to think or concentrate, and recurrent thoughts of death including suicidal ideation with or without a plan. Suicide is the most serious and acute risk for patients with major depressive disorder, so physicians should ask detailed questions about patients ' suicidal ideation and previous suicide attempts when there is any suggestion of suicidality.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Career planning and college preparedness (Choice A) is not necessary for the physician to address at this time with this patient. The physician may choose to address these topics with older adolescents as they prepare to transition out of their childhood homes, particularly if changes in location as a result of college could potentia lly lead to interruptions in the care of chronic medica l conditions. Choking hazards and poisoning prevention (Choice B) is a necessary part of counse ling during the well-child examination of an infant or toddler. However, these risks are not likely to cause harm in an adolescent. Vitamin D and folic acid supplementation (Choice D) is not necessary in this patient with a healthy, well-rounded diet and lack of other medical comorbidities.

questionStem: A 75-year-o ld man comes to the physician with his wife because of a 1-day history of severe lower abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting , and an inabi lity to urinate. Six months ago , the patie nt's wife began to notice that he was taking longer than usua l to urinate and leavi ng drops of urine on the toilet bowl rim and floor. During the past 5 days, he has made frequent trips to the bathroom and often has needed to return short ly after voiding. He has type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertens ion, and stage 2 chronic kidney disease . His medications are glipizide, glargine insulin, and amlodipine. Exam ination shows suprapubic tenderness. Labo ratory stud ies show: Serum Na+ K+ cI ­ Hco -3 Urea nitrogen Creatin ine Urine pH Specific grav ity Blood Glucose Bilirubin Protein Ketones Nitrites Leukocy te esterase Urob ilinogen 140 mEq/L 4.1 mEq/L 101 mEq/L 25 mEq/L 23 mg/dL 3.4 mg/dL 6.3 1.015 1+ negative negative 30 mg/dL negative 1+ 1+ 0.2 mg/dL (N<2) Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's current symptoms?

Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) affects middle-aged and elderly male patients and occurs because of excess growth of tissue in the central zone of the prostate causing lower urinary tract obstruction. BPH presents with urinary dribbling and incontinence, difficulty starting or maintaining a urinary stream, nocturia, the need to frequently urinate, and incomplete voiding. These symptoms are typically insidious in onset, chronic, and progressive. Chronic outlet obstruction leads to urinary retention and may cause hydronephrosis or urinary tract infection. The diagnosis of BPH is made by history, physical, and urodynamic testing, along with ruling out of alternate diagnoses (eg, prostatic malignancy). Treatment is with supportive care, a-blockers (eg, tamsulosin), 5-a-reductase inhibitors (eg, finasteride), or surgery. Urinary tract infections associated with BPH are treated with antibiotics (eg, trimethoprim, sulfamethoxazole, or nitrofuran toin).

Granular, muddy brown casts are typica l on urinalysis. Dehydration (Choice C) may lead to kidney injury and may increase the risk for urinary tract infection but does not present with chronic urinary frequency or urgency, which are suggestive of urinary tract outlet obstruction secondary to BPH. Nephrolithiasis (Choice D) presents with colicky flank pain radiating to the groin, gross hematuria, and difficulty voiding. This patient's chronic history of urinary frequency and hesitancy is more suggestive of BPH. Progression of hypertensive nephropathy (Choice E) would lead to a reduction in glomerular filtration rate and reduced urinary output. It would not lead to suprapubic tenderness, urinary hesitancy or frequency. Incomplete voiding and urinary retention increase the risk for urinary tract infection in patients with benign prostatic hyperplasia.

questionStem: A 17-year-old girl comes to the office for an annual well-child examination. Her last visit to the physician was 14 months ago, during which she received one dose of the quadrivalent human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. During the past 2 years, she has been sexually active with one male partner; they use condoms consistently. Examination shows no abnormal ities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in manageme nt regarding the HPV vaccine?

choices.A: Readministratio n of the first dose of the vaccine today with a recommendat ion that the patient receive a second dose in 2 months and a
choices.B: Administration of a second dose of the vaccine today with a recommendation that the patient receive a third dose in 4 months
choices.C: Administratio n of the last dose of the vaccine today

correctExplanation: The patient should receive administration of the second dose of the HPV vaccine today with a recommendation to receive a third dose in four months. HPV is a common human pathogen that infects epithelial cells. There are multiple strains, both low- and high-risk for the development of squamous cell carcinoma, which result in the deve lopment of a variety of lesions including cervical cancer, condylomata acuminata, verruca vulgaris, plantar warts, and mucosa! lesions of the oropharynx, respiratory epithelium, and larynx. HPV is primarily transmitted through genita l contact. The quadriva lent vaccine is one of three HPV vaccines and covers four serotypes: HPV types 6, 11, 16, and 18. Routine vaccination against HPV is recommended at age 11 to 12 or as young as age 9. In a patient who receives their first dose of quadriva lent HPV vaccine after age 15, three doses are recommended, ideally at months 0, 2, and 6. Doses may be administered after these minimum intervals, so this patient, who is 12 months late for her second dose, can still receive the dose today and the third dose in four months. Only two doses are needed in patients who received the first dose when younger than age 15.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Readministration of the first dose today (Choice A) is not necessary. She can still receive the second and third doses of the immunization despite it having been over a year since her first dose. Doses of the quadrivalent HPV vaccine only need to be readministered if they were given before the minimum time interval passed. Administration of the last dose of the vaccine today (Choice C) would leave the patient only partially vaccinated. Because her first dose was after the age of 15, she needs two more doses, not one. No further management (Choice D) is not appropriate as the patient is only partially vaccinated for HPV serotypes 6, 11, 16, and 18. Two additiona l doses are required to achieve the maximum effect.

questionStem: A 20-month-o ld boy is broug ht to the office by his mother because she is conce rned about his speech. She says he babbles various sounds but makes no words. He was born at term to a 26-year-old primigravid woman following an uncomp licated pregnancy and sponta neous vagina l delivery. Apgar scores were 8 a nd 9 at 1 and 5 minutes, respectively. He has no history of serious illness and receives no medicat ions. The patient 's grandmother assists with child care while the mother works part-time at a clothing store. The patient lives in a house constructed in 1938. He is at the 35th percenti le for length and weight. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examina tion shows no abnormalities. He is active and respo nds to aural and tactile stimuli. He has limited direct eye contact, makes babbling sounds, and does not say any words. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Autism spectrum disorder is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by a broad range of signs and symptoms involving restricted and repetitive patterns of behavior or activities, difficulties with socia l interaction, and difficulties with communication. Children with autism often display a lack of interest in others, failure in empathy, and challenging behavior. The clinica l manifestations of autism spectrum disorder typically present within the first 2 years of life with delayed or regression of comm unication or social skills. Impaired social cognition includes impaired nonverbal comm unication such as eye contact and facial expressions. Management of autism spectrum disorder is individualized depending on the clinical manifestations and degree of impairmen t of the patient. Therapy involves behavioral, developmental, social, and educational interventions to improve socia l functioning, communica tion skills, and academic functioning.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Down syndrome (Choice B) results from trisomy of chromosome 21 and presents with charac teristic physical feature s including broad, flat, facial features with prominent epicanthal folds, and a single palmar crease. Patients with Down syndrome are at increased risk for dementia, Alzheimer type , acute lymphob lastic and acute myeloid leukem ia, cardiac septa! defects, duodenal atresia, and Hirschsprung disease. Failure to thrive (Choice C) in an infant is characterized by inadequate or abnormal pattern of weight gain and can be caused by inadequate caloric intake , malnutrition, inborn errors of metabolism, hyperthyroidism, among other disorders. This patient is at 35th percentile for length and weight which is normal.

questionStem: A 37-yea r-old man comes to the office because of a 1-week history of visual disturbances, flashing lights, and blurred vision. He tested positive for HIV infection 8 years ago. He has not been taking his antiretrov iral med ications during the past 4 months, explaining, "I just got tired of the daily routine." His temperature is 37.1 °C (98.8°F), pulse is 84/min, respira tions are 16/min, and blood pressure is 128/76 mm Hg. Physical exam ination discloses no abnormal ities. Which of the following is the most likely infectious agent?
correctExplanation: Cytomegalovirus (CMV), also known as human herpesvirus-5 (HHV-5), is an opportunistic infection common ly occurring in immunocompromised patients. It can cause a variety of presentations, including mononucleosis in immuno competent patients, and retinitis, esophagitis, and pneumonia in immunocompromised patients. Retinitis occurs in HIV infection or AIDS when the CD4+ T lymphocyte count is low (often less than 50 cells/ml) and presents with blurred vision, blind spots, flashing lights, or floaters, most common ly unilateral. Symptoms are caused by CMV-induced retinal inflammation , necrosis, and edema, which can lead to retinal detachment and blindness if untreated. Treatments include intravitreal and systemic antivira l therapy.

Cryptococcus neoformans (Choice A) is an encapsu lated yeast and common opportunistic pathogen in immunocompromised patients, especially patients with HIV infection or AIDS and CD4+ T lymphocytes counts less than 200 cells/ml. Infection can cause pulmonary cryptoco ccosis, meningitis, and encephalitis. Cryptosporidium parvum (Choice B) causes self-limited watery diarrhea in immunocompetent patients. In patients with HIV infection or other immuno suppression, however, the disease can cause profound weight loss and dehydration. Rubella virus (Choice D) presents with fever, arthralgias, and lymphadenopathy (most often postauricu lar) with a confluent rash that spreads from the head to the trunk and then to the extremities. Congenita l rubella can cause retinitis but infection in adulthood does not. questionStem: A previous ly healthy ?-year-old boy is brought to the physician because he started limping on his left leg 3 days ago and now refuses to bear weight on it. The mother says that he has "felt feverish" to touch. He has no history of recent trauma. He is at the 45th percentile for height and the 60th percenti le for weight. His temperatu re is 38.9°C (102°F), pulse is 108/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 110/72 mm Hg. The patient holds the left hip flexed, abducted, and externa lly rotated. Passive and active range of motion of the left hip is limited by pain. The left sacroiliac joint is nontender to palpation. Laboratory studies show a leukocyte count of 15,500/mm 3, erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 110 mm/h, and a serum C-reactive protein concentrat ion of 4.2 mg/L (N=0.08-3.1 ). Which of the following is the most likely diagnos is?
correctExplanation: Septic arthritis results from bacterial infection of the synovia l joint space, most commonly by Staphylococcus aureus. Patients typically present with fever, reduced range of motion of the affected joint, and refusal to bear weight. While the hip may appear normal, affected knee joints may appear swollen and erythematous. Serum laboratory features common ly include leukocytosis and increased concentrations of inflammatory markers, including erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein. Arthrocentesis is indicated for the evaluation of monoarticu lar erythema and swelling to evaluate for septic arthritis, which characteristically discloses purulent synovial fluid with >50,000 leukocytes/mm 3. Treatment includes operative management and antibiotic coverage of empiric pathogens (eg, vancomycin and a third-generation cepha losporin).
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Acute rheumatic fever (Choice A) presents with migratory polyarthralgia, pancarditis (pericarditis, myocarditis, or endocarditis), subcutaneous nodules, erythema marginatum, Sydenham chorea, fever, increased erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and short PR interval following an infection from group A streptococci, most often pharyngitis. Legg-Calve-Perthes disease (Choice B) refers to idiopathic avascular necrosis of the femora l head that most commonly occurs in younger boys from 4 to 9 years old. The classic presentation includes the slow onset of hip pain which is worsened by activity and associated with a limp. It does not present with fever or leukocytosis. Slipped capital femoral epiphysis (Choice D) most common ly occurs in overweight children between the ages of 10 and 15 years. It results in displacement of the femoral epiphysis relative to the femoral neck caused by a fracture of the growth plate.

questionStem: A 67-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 2-month history of fatigue and increased urine output. She has hypertension treated with enalapril. Her blood pressure is 143/88 mm Hg. Examination shows no other abnormalities. Laboratory studies show: Serum Ca2+ Phosphorus Albumin Urine specific gravity Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnos is?

choices.C: Measurement of serum parathyroid hormone concentration
choices.D: Measureme nt of serum vitamin D concentration

correctExplanation: 11.9 mg/dl 2.1 mg/dl 4.8 g/dl 1.005 Primary hyperparathyroidism presents with hypercalcemia (which in turn presents with nephrolithiasis, chronic bone pain, abdominal discomfort, and psychiatric disturbances), hypophosphatemia, subperiostea l bone resorption, and end-stage kidney disease. Excessive production of parathyroid hormone (PTH) results in increased serum calcium concentration from increased osteoclast activity, intestinal absorption, and renal tubular absorption. Serum phosphorus concentration is decreased secondary to increased excretion by the renal tubules. Patients with laboratory findings concerning for hyperparathyroidism, such as this patient with hypercalcemia and hypophosphatemia, should undergo further evaluation with the measurement of serum parathyroid hormone concentration. Once confirmed, imaging studies may localize a parathyroid adenoma, hyperplasia, or carcinoma.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Glucose tolerance testing (Choice A) is useful for the diagnosis of diabetes mellitus. While diabetes mellitus may also present with increased urination, it does not cause hypercalcemia and hypophosphatemia. Urine culture (Choice B) is useful for the diagnosis of urinary tract infection (UTI). While UTI may present with increased urination, it is typically accompanied by other symptoms such as dysuria, urgency, and suprapubic tenderness. UTls do not typically cause hypercalcemia and hypophosphatemia.

questionStem: A 22-year-old woman comes to the physician in January because of a 6-week history of an itching, burning rash over her forearms and wrists. She has a history of similar rashes around this time of year but says that this rash is the worst she has ever experienced. Two weeks ago, she had an upper respiratory tract infection that resolved spontaneous ly. She has no other history of serious illness and takes no medications. A photograph of the right upper extremity is shown. These findings also appear over the volar aspect of the wrists. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: Gentle skin care and frequent use of topical moisturizing cream is the initial step in managing atopic dermatitis (AD). AD, or eczema, is a chronic pruritic inflammatory skin disease common in children that is suggested by a personal or family history of atopic disease (eg, asthma or allergic rhinitis). It may persist into adulthood or, less commonly, may even arise in adulthood. The rash is initially characterized by erythematous papules and vesicles with exudates and crusting and, with chronic scratching, becomes dry, scaly, and excoriated in a process called lichenification. AD patients tend to have generalized background dryness, or xerosis. AD patients should be counseled to use fragrance-free products, avoid bathing in hot water, and apply emollient (or moisturizing cream) daily. In patients whose eczema persists despite these interventions, a mid-potency topical corticosteroid such as triamcinolone acetonide 0.1 % is appropriate. Topical corticosteroids which are more potent, such as betamethasone or clobetaso l, should be used with caution and avoided all together in children where the risk for systemic absorption as a result of increased body surface area ratio is higher.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Oral cyclosporine therapy (Choice A) and oral methotrexate therapy (Choice B) are both immunosuppressive agents which can be used to treat severe AD. With the advent of biologic medications for AD, the need for immunosuppressants in the management of AD has decreased. Systemic therapies for AD are indicated when conservative measures including topical corticosteroids have failed, body surface area involvement exceeds 10%, or the dermatitis severely impacts the patient's daily functioning. In this case, the eczema is limited to a relatively small area on the arms and wrists and conservative management has not yet been attempted. Topical ketoconazo le cream (Choice C) is an antifungal medication used to treat superficia l dermatophyte infections such as tinea corporis, tinea pedis, or tinea cruris. AD can be distinguished from tinea corporis by its lack of annular scaly patches and its classic distribution involving the flexural surfaces, as in this patient. - • • I I - •• soriasis. questionStem: A 25-year-o ld man comes to the physician for evaluation 2 days after his sexual partner was diagnosed with acute hepatitis B. Examination shows no abnorma lities. Three days later, laboratory studies show: Hepatitis B surface antigen Antibody to hepatitis B surface antigen Antibody to hepatitis B core antigen negative negative negative In addition to condom use counseling, which of the following is the most appropriate recomme ndation to prevent hepatitis B in this patient?

choices.C: Hepatitis B immune globulin and hepatitis B vaccine series

correctExplanation: Hepatitis B is transmitted through blood, sexual contact, or perinatally. Chronic infection can lead to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma. Vaccination against hepatitis B is commonly given to newborns, although it can also be given in adulthood and is recommended for healthcare workers, injection drug users, men who have sex with men, and patients with HIV infection or hepatitis C. A patient that has received their vaccination will have antibodies to the hepatitis B surface antigen. This patient has no antibody to hepatitis B surface antigen, which indicates that he never received a complete vaccination. Additionally, he does not have active infection given his negative hepatitis B surface antigen. Absence of antibody against the hepatitis B core antigen also confirms that this patient has not previously been infected with hepatitis B. Therefore, the most appropriate next step in this patient is to prevent infection from this exposure with hepatitis B immune globulin and prevent future infection with the hepatitis B vaccine series.
incorrectExplanation: nd H. Hepatitis B immune globulin only (Choice A) would prevent this patient from developing hepatitis B in response to this exposure. However, it would not prevent infection from future exposures.

questionStem: A 47-year-o ld woman comes to the physician because of nonproductive, "bothersome" cough almost every day for 2 months, especia lly at night. Her symptoms have not responded to a 4-week course of antihistam ines and decongestants. She has not had fever, shortness of breath, or any other symptoms. She has hypothyroidism well controlled with levothyroxine. There is no family history of serious illness. She has smoked one-ha lf pack of cigarettes daily for 25 years. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 60/min and regular, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 110/76 mm Hg. The oropharynx appears normal with no cobbleston ing. Cardiopulmonary exam ination shows no abnorma lities. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's cough?
correctExplanation: The most common causes of chronic cough are gastroesophagea l reflux disease (GERO), asthma, and postnasal drip. Distinguishing among these causes requires a careful history and physical examination. GERO is most likely in this patient whose symptoms are exacerbated by supine positioning, not associated with shortness of breath, and not responsive to antihistamines or decongestants. GERO is caused by decreased lower esophagea l sphincter tone or increased intra-abdomina l pressure that causes acidic gastric contents to reflux into the esophagus. It typica lly presents with burning epigastric and lower chest pain, a sour or metallic taste, and nausea, although it can present solely with a nocturnal cough, as in this patient. Treatment includes proton pump inhibitors or H 2 receptor antagonists. Complications of untreated GERO include the development of reflux esophagitis, esophagea l strictures, Barrett esophagus, and esophagea l adenocarcinoma.

However, the cough would be expected to improve with antihistamines and decongestants. Additiona lly, postnasal drip is commonly associated with cobblestoning of the oropharynx on physical examination. Emphysema (Choice C) occurs in patients with significant smoking history and presents with exertional dyspnea, cough, wheezing, and sputum production. This patient has only a 12 1 /2 pack-year history and has no dyspnea or sputum production, making emphysema unlikely. questionStem: A 66-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 1-year history of shortness of breath with exertion and progressive cough productive of small amounts of white sputum. He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. He has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 50 years. Vital signs are within normal limits. Pulse oximetry on room air shows a resting oxygen saturation of 91 %; his oxygen saturation is 89% with ambulation. Pulmonary examination shows a prolonged expiratory phase. Prior spirometry shows a baseline FEV 1 of 55% of predicted and an FEV 1:FVC ratio of 60%. The FEV 1 improved by 15% after administration of a bronchodilator. Which of the following is most likely to prevent worsening of this patient's underlying condition?

choices.A: Combined inhaled corticosteroid and long-acting ~-adrenergic agonist therapy

correctExplanation: Smoking cessation is the most likely intervention to prevent worsening of this patient's obstructive lung disease. Long-term smokers are at risk for numerous diseases of the lung including chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), which is diagnosed by spirometry when the FEV 1:FVC ratio is less than 70%. The severity of the obstruction is graded depending upon the severity in reduction of the FEV 1. An FEV 1 of 55% is classified as moderate obstruction. Other common symptoms include dyspnea on exertion and productive cough. Treatment focuses on preventing further decline in respiratory function though smoking cessation in addition to the use of medications such as inhaled antimuscarinics, short and long-acting ~-adrenergic agonists, and corticosteroids. Patients with resting or ambulatory saturation less than 88% are also candidates for oxygen therapy.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Combined inhaled corticosteroid and long-acting ~-adrenergic agonist therapy (Choice A) is used as step-up therapy for patients who continue to have symptoms despite use of antimuscarinics or long-acting ~-adrenergic agonists. It does not prevent worsening of the underlying disease. Long-acting anticholinergic therapy (Choice B) is a good initial pharmacologic choice for patients with COPD, but the first step in treatment for this patient should be smoking cessation. Anticholinergic therapy does not prevent worsening of the underlying disease. Long-term, low-dose oral corticosteroid therapy (Choice C) is rarely indicated to treat COPD. Acute exacerbations of COPD are often treated with short courses of high-dose prednisone.
